opus-5.5.text:
I think the basic mechanism is pretty straightforward once you look at how the semiconductor supply chain actually responds to demand signals. Building out chip production capacity is enormously capital intensive. A leading-edge fab costs on the order of $20 billion or more, and then you have all the upstream pieces: lithography tools, advanced packaging, high-bandwidth memory. Companies like TSMC, ASML, and the memory makers are historically quite conservative about expanding capacity, because the semiconductor industry has a long history of boom-and-bust cycles. They've been burned before by overbuilding and then watching prices collapse.

So what they're really looking for is evidence that demand is durable. Revenue alone isn't quite enough. If AI labs are spending a lot on compute but burning cash to do it, a supplier might reasonably worry that this is a bubble funded by investor enthusiasm that could dry up. But if AI products are generating healthy margins, if every dollar of compute turns into substantially more than a dollar of value captured, that's a much stronger signal. It tells the supply chain the spending is self-sustaining and likely to keep growing.

Higher margins also directly fund the investment. Labs and hyperscalers with strong cash flows can sign long-term purchase commitments and prepay for capacity, which shifts risk off the suppliers and makes them much more willing to build. We've already seen some of this, with hyperscalers committing huge capex budgets and helping finance expansion in packaging and memory.

There's a feedback loop here too. More profitable AI means more willingness to pay for chips, which raises chip margins, which justifies more fabs, which over time brings down compute costs and enables more capable systems that are themselves more profitable. So the profitability of AI deployment is one of the key variables determining how fast that whole flywheel spins. In a world where AI is very valuable but someone, maybe through competition, maybe through other frictions, can't capture much of that value as profit, you'd expect a noticeably slower buildout than in a world where the returns are clearly visible on the balance sheet.

r001.rationale: The response says higher AI margins, purchase commitments, and prepayments can encourage capacity expansion, but it does not state that spending far above normal chip-production costs would accelerate supply.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss human-wage income from running an already-developed human-level AI model or use that income to justify paying substantially more for chips than buyers pay today.

fable-5.1.text:
Sure. So the basic idea is that the supply of AI chips right now is constrained not really by physics or by any hard limit, but by how much the whole supply chain is willing to invest. And that willingness is downstream of expected returns.

Think about what it actually takes to produce a leading-edge accelerator. You need TSMC or another foundry to build fabs, which cost tens of billions of dollars each and take years to come online. You need ASML to ramp EUV lithography tools. You need packaging capacity, CoWoS in particular, which has been one of the real bottlenecks. You need HBM from SK Hynix, Samsung, Micron. Every one of those players is making a bet when they expand capacity. They're committing enormous capital years ahead of when the revenue shows up, and they're exposed if demand turns out to be softer than they expected. The semiconductor industry has a long memory of boom and bust cycles, so there's a lot of institutional caution built in.

Now, if AI labs and the companies deploying AI are earning high margins, that changes the calculus in a couple of ways. First, it's a direct demand signal. High margins mean the labs can afford to pay a lot for compute, and they'll keep paying for it, because each marginal chip is generating more value than it costs. So the foundries and the equipment makers see sustained, credible demand rather than a speculative spike. That makes them much more willing to pull forward capacity expansions they'd otherwise stage out over a longer horizon.

Second, high margins can be shared up the supply chain. If Nvidia is earning very large margins on its chips, that's partly because the downstream applications are valuable enough to sustain those prices. And Nvidia can then afford to prepay TSMC, sign long-term supply agreements, co-invest in packaging capacity, and so on. We've actually seen some of this. These kinds of commitments de-risk the capacity buildout for suppliers, because now someone else is absorbing part of the downside.

Third, and I think this is underappreciated, high profits attract entry. If the margins in AI compute are very high, that's a signal to AMD, to the hyperscalers building their own silicon, to startups, to Chinese firms, that there's a lot of money on the table. Competition takes time to materialize because the lead times are so long, but over a horizon of several years it meaningfully expands total supply.

So the chain of reasoning is roughly: AI generates economic value, that shows up as profit margins, those margins justify paying high prices for compute, and those prices propagate backward through a supply chain that's fundamentally capital-constrained and risk-averse, and loosen that constraint. The reverse is also true, which is worth keeping in mind. If AI revenue disappoints relative to the capex that's already been committed, you'd expect the buildout to slow down quite sharply. So it's not that chips just automatically get cheaper and more plentiful over time. It's quite sensitive to whether the economics at the application layer actually work out.

r001.rationale: The response says high margins can support high compute prices and encourage supply-chain investment, but does not state that buyers spending far above normal chip-production costs would accelerate chip supply.

r002.rationale: The response does not connect chip prices to human-wage income from running an already-developed human-level AI model or say that this could justify paying substantially more than buyers pay today.

astra-6.text:
Higher profit margins mean there’s more money available to invest in compute, and they make those investments more attractive. If an AI company can earn a lot from each additional chip it deploys, it has a strong incentive to buy more chips, and it can afford to pay more for them.

That sends a signal up the supply chain. Chip designers, manufacturers, and suppliers of things like memory and packaging see stronger demand and a greater potential return from expanding capacity. AI companies can also support that expansion through long-term purchase commitments or upfront payments, which reduce the risk for suppliers.

Of course, you can’t build a semiconductor fab overnight. There are physical constraints and substantial lead times. But higher margins can make it worthwhile to invest in relieving those constraints sooner, so chip supply grows faster than it otherwise would.

r001.rationale: The response says higher margins can make buyers willing to pay more and encourage capacity expansion, but it does not state that spending far above normal chip-production costs could accelerate supply.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention human-wage income from running an already-developed human-level AI model or use it to justify paying substantially more than buyers pay today.

sol-6.1.text:
Higher profit margins mean that AI companies can afford to pay more for chips while still making a profit. So if chips are scarce, they can bid up the price, and that creates a stronger incentive for suppliers to expand production.

That can happen at several points in the supply chain: investing in more fabrication capacity, expanding advanced packaging, or producing more high-bandwidth memory. Higher prices can also make it worthwhile to redirect existing capacity toward AI chips.

Of course, some of these investments take years, so you don’t get an immediate increase in supply. But the important point is that chip supply isn’t fixed. If providing AI services is sufficiently profitable, that creates a powerful economic incentive to overcome those bottlenecks.

r001.rationale: The response says higher margins can let AI companies bid up scarce chip prices and encourage more production, but it does not state that spending far above normal chip-production costs would accelerate supply.

r002.rationale: The response does not discuss human-wage income from running an already-developed human-level AI model or justify paying substantially more for its chips than buyers pay today.
